passages.t: ‘If only My people would listen to Me’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. According to Gittith. Of Asaph” (verse 1). It begins as a festival song. “Sing for joy to God our strength; make a joyful noise to the God of Jacob” (verse 1). Bring the drum, the harp and the lyre (verse 2). “Sound the ram's horn at the New Moon, and at the full moon on the day of our Feast” (verse 3).

Then the music stops and God speaks. He remembers Egypt: “I relieved his shoulder of the burden; his hands were freed from the basket” (verse 6). He remembers rescue and testing in the desert (verse 7).

Then he pleads. “Hear, O My people, and I will warn you: O Israel, if only you would listen to Me” (verse 8). Have no other god (verse 9). “I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of Egypt. Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it” (verse 10).

“But My people would not listen to Me” (verse 11). So God let them go their own way (verse 12). Yet he still longs for them. “If only My people would listen to Me” (verse 13). He would feed them the finest wheat and “honey from the rock” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
‘Gittith’ also heads Psalms 8 and 84. No one is sure what it means. Some link it with the city of Gath, others with the word for a wine press.

The New Moon began each month, and the full moon fell in the middle. Which feast verse 3 means is debated. Many think of the feasts of the seventh month, the trumpets at the new moon and the Feast of Tabernacles at the full moon. Others think of Passover, which also began at the full moon and remembers Egypt. The psalm does not say.

The ram's horn, the shofar, was not played for a tune. It was a signal, to call the people together.

The ‘basket’ (verse 6) recalls the slavery in Egypt, carrying clay and bricks. ‘Meribah’ (verse 7) means ‘quarrelling’. It was the place where the people demanded water and tested God (Exodus 17:7).

Verses 9 and 10 echo the first words of the Ten Commandments, sung back to the people at a feast: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2).
passages.later:
Jesus grieved over Jerusalem with the same longing: “how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

Hebrews warns, “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15). Paul says that God ‘gave them over’ to their own desires (Romans 1:24), much as verse 12 does.
passages.asks:
Psalm 81 lets you hear God's side of the story. He is not cold. He says ‘if only’, twice. He wants to fill your mouth with good things.

So ask yourself: where am I not listening? It may be in the middle of worship, when the music is loud and joyful, that God most wants you to stop and hear him.
